content:
Should we allow LLM-generated code in the Seymour project?

We didn't need generative AI for the easy direction. Should we use it for the hard direction?
Allowing LLM code will diminish any benefits of the project in my opinion

I would say: it depends on what the project goals are, and there are practical considerations.
project goals: If it's "just have any sorry-free proof of the full theorem", AI is of course fine. On the other hand, I'd argue this is probably the wrong goal. "X can be formalised" is a rather weak signal (people in this community have believed this for years), "X has been formalised in any way" is not interesting in the age of AI. "We have formalised X and learned something about the mathematics and/or the best design for the formalisation" is interesting. "We have formalised X and advanced mathlib in this area" also is. For the latter, bashing through with AI is not that helpful.

In the Carleson project, we had this split between ToMathlib (i.e., code that should be reusable and eventually go into mathlib), with its high stanards. Allowing AI there would be counterproductive. In the Carleson directory, the standard was pretty much "anything goes" (that is not malicious, compiles in reasonable time, etc.) For such a directory, allowing AI seems fine.
I don't know what fraction of Seymour is ToMathlib or Carleson.

Practical considerations: you want to be sure definitions are correct (i.e., write them by hand), and need to be able to maintain all the code. This will inform whether you want to accept a particular piece of AI-written code.

Finally: mathlib's AI policy reserves the right to close low-quality PRs (if these are too burdensome on the maintainers). This will probably be less relevant, but you may want to think if this applies to you also.

At the moment formalizing the hard direction rests upon first formalizing big things all of which are of great interest to Mathlib (planar graphs, menger's theorem, splitter theorem, Kuratowski, etc), so at the very least we have to do these by hand and this is a lot of work already.

Michael Rothgang said:

I would say: it depends on what the project goals are, and there are practical considerations.
project goals: If it's "just have any sorry-free proof of the full theorem", AI is of course fine.

I don't have a good answer to the question what the goals are.

When we were starting the work, "just have any sorry-free proof of the full theorem" was sufficiently ambitious and sufficiently interesting. However, the times have changed. Right now, I don't have a good concept of what an interesting project in 2026 is.

I don't have a good answer to the question what the goals are.

Then that would be my first question to you, as an outsider :-)

I think formalising a new area is still interesting --- provided you're interested in a good formalisation. E.g., aim for sufficiently generality, later reusability and abstraction (perhaps even mathlib!), take note of design trade-offs and discuss the best ones, etc.

Michael Rothgang said:

Practical considerations: you want to be sure definitions are correct (i.e., write them by hand), and need to be able to maintain all the code. This will inform whether you want to accept a particular piece of AI-written code.

We have already checked thoroughly that definitions are correct. The hard direction has been fully stated. The remaining task is to prove it.

Michael Rothgang said:

sufficiently generality

The first design decision @Ivan S. and I made was to aim for low generality.

Not very exciting to hear in the year of the lord 2026, I know!

Hey!

As a part of a school project, I worked on the last remaining sorry of the easy direction. However, it has come to my attention now, that the project is apparently LLM-free? My code is not, as I use gemini as a de-facto copilot, often copy-pasting the goal there to get some guidance on how to continue. The vast majority of the code is still hand written (80%+), but LLM was indeed used in the rest.

The question for you is if you want to accept the PR and the code to become part of your codebase or not.

If nobody objects, I'll merge it.

Perhaps a comment at the beginning on the file (the only file that was LLM-assisted) that LLMs were used?
